THOUGHT: This 55-year-old male presents with systemic “B symptoms” (fever is absent, but night sweats, weight loss >10% body weight or >10 kg — here ~5.4 kg over ~4 weeks, and fatigue are highly suggestive), along with lymphadenopathy (enlarged, nontender, fixed supraclavicular node — a classic “Virchow’s node” sign often associated with abdominal or thoracic malignancy), splenomegaly, abdominal distension/fullness, and left lower quadrant dullness (suggesting splenic enlargement or possibly bulky retroperitoneal disease). The CT shows widespread lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, mediastinal), consistent with disseminated lymphoid malignancy. CBC shows elevated WBC (possible lymphocytosis or reactive process, though not specified as absolute count or differential), mildly decreased hemoglobin (anemia of chronic disease or marrow infiltration), normal platelets (early stage or non-marrow-infiltrative pattern). Elevated LDH is a well-recognized tumor burden and poor-prognosis marker in lymphomas. Critically, the cervical lymph node biopsy reveals lymphocytes with high proliferative index and CD20 positivity — indicating a B-cell origin. CD20+ B-cell lymphoma with systemic symptoms, bulky nodal disease, extranodal involvement (spleen), and B symptoms strongly points to aggressive B-cell lymphoma. While several subtypes exist (e.g., DLBCL, Burkitt, PMBCL), the most common, most likely diagnosis in this age group with this clinical-radiologic-pathologic presentation — especially with diffuse large nodes, splenomegaly, B symptoms, and CD20+ high-grade morphology — is Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). Other considerations like Hodgkin lymphoma are less likely: HL typically shows Reed-Sternberg cells (not mentioned), and CD20 is only variably positive (and usually not uniformly strong); also, HL less commonly causes massive splenomegaly without hepatic involvement or such prominent abdominal symptoms. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) is less likely given the high proliferative index, aggressive symptom onset (4-week progression), bulky disease, and absence of lymphocytosis in CBC description. Mantle cell lymphoma could present similarly but is less common and often has cyclin D1 positivity (not tested here); however, DLBCL remains the most prevalent aggressive lymphoma and best fits the totality.

DIAGNOSIS: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
